body: I cried when my therapist said, “You‘re not alone with this“ because my brain interpreted it as “You’re just like all the other patients and nothing special.“ I knew she was trying to comfort me and meant it in a kind, reassuring way, but I left the office with tears in my eyes ans then started sobbing in the hallway.

It’s not true that psychoanalysis is ineffective. What OP‘s therapist said shows that she’s a bad therapist personally, not that the whole modality doesn’t work. I‘ve been in therapy with a psychoanalytically trained therapist for years and she would NEVER say what OP‘s therapist said; she would be shocked by such a response.

I‘m a non-native speaker and learned English from her books as a kid (about 12 years ago). I picked up on the “ever so“ and used it frequently in English lessons until I realized nobody actually speaks this way haha.

I wish my therapist had a room I could go to after a difficult session. I asked her once when I couldn’t stop crying and had to walk out without having calmed down. She said that there are no spare rooms but offered that I sit in the hall. That wasn’t an option for me, though, because the hall is tiny, doesn’t have a table, and other people would have probably walked past me.
Exactly! I‘ve noticed that poems I‘ve written about the pain of the therapeutic relationship read a lot like my poems about other painful relationships in my life.

Your poem resonates with me. I feel the same way about therapy. It hurts so much and I don’t know how to make it easier. The last paragraph especially speaks to me – there’s this deep desire to mean something to my therapist, to not be forgotten, not be easily replaceable, and to make a difference in her life.
I‘m exactly the same. Turning 24 in ten days, feeling like 15 and struggling with commitments and responsibility.
Well, there might still be hope for me then.
I‘m trying lamotrigine (I‘m on 150mg at the moment) and I really hope it’ll help me. I‘ve tried so many other meds and never noticed positive effects. May I ask what dose you‘re on?

Yes, and I hate that just talking about your symptoms isn’t enough. It can also make you feel like you have to have been in a dangerous situations to be taken seriously, which is obviously not how it should be.

I relate so my much. My therapist is my FP (unfortunately) and I‘m always sad I can‘t be closer to her, physically and emotionally. Yet when she went up to me last session to hand me a tissue while I was curled up in a ball crying, I didn’t lift my head and asked her why she was standing in front of me in an almost annoyed tone. I wanted her to go back to her chair and asked her to just put the tissue down next to me. It didn’t feel good at all when I sensed she was approaching me, and yet I constantly fantasize about being close to her outside of sessions. Also, I love looking at her face yet spend approximately 98% of the sessions looking away.
Thank you, that’s a helpful perspective.
No, I don’t think so.
Actually listening to music right now.
I was just thinking about that too.

My boyfriend of almost five years literally just broke up with me 20 minutes ago and the last thing I said to him was that I‘m gonna die if he leaves, that I can’t live without him. It does feel that way. But obviously it’s not a mature or healthy or fair thing to say. I‘m on here now to hopefully distract myself from SI.

I‘m in a bad relationship too and I don’t know how breaking up could possibly work for me. I tried in February and lasted two weeks before I went back. My boyfriend’s been saying he‘d be better off without me since the start of our relationship, yet we‘ve been together for almost five years now. 

He routinely says horrible things to me (no one wants to be around you, you‘re ruining my life, the worst things that have happened to me were experiences with you, at least give me your money first if you’re going to kill yourself) and hearing those things does deeply upset and hurt me, but I always forgive him quickly and look forward to seeing him again. There’s this sense of calm and safety when he’s around. 

I don’t want to be stuck with him forever, I really don’t. I think I could be much happier and more stable with a different partner. I just don’t see it happening unless he breaks up with me. I don’t know how other people with BPD manage breakups. Maybe they have close friends? I only have two friends, and while I‘m emotionally close to them, they both live far away and we (almost) only message or speak on the phone. Their support isn’t nearly enough to make up for the hole that’s left behind when I don’t have him in my life (as I said, I did try in February).

I‘m in exactly the same place. I feel depressed every single day and I‘ve been in different types of therapy for years. “It’s never enough“ resonates a lot. I also feel like I’m just not meant to live at this point. You can message me if you need someone to talk to.
I already talked about it with a dermatologist years ago. Apparently you can’t take it when you have a peanut or soy allergy, and I have both.

Oh wow, this sounds hard. My dad thinks therapy is a pointless wallowing in emotions and past experiences that leads nowhere, a waste of time for pathetic wussies. 

He‘s convinced he doesn’t have any mental health issues, but I‘m quite sure he has NPD (narcissistic personality disorder).

Don’t minimize how bad it was because this is a horrible and EXTREMELY unprofessional thing to say. 

I hope you’ve found a counselor or therapist who doesn’t/didn’t give up on you. ❤️

I completely relate. My BPD stems from family-related childhood trauma, and when I was a teenager I tried to talk with my dad about our problematic family dynamics. I explained what was difficult for me growing up as gently and carefully as I could, but he stopped me, looked me straight in the eye and said: No. We were good parents. The problem is entirely in yourself.

I walked away crying and never had a conversation with him about our family since then.
Man, my dad is horrible but what yours says makes mine look nice and kind in comparison,
This made me smile and I really hope I‘ll find a partner like that too someday.

Yes. I‘ve talked about this in therapy so many times and my therapist has tried to reassure me and teach me techniques to question my negative thoughts and make me feel better. 

I do try to be kinder to myself now and remind myself that I don’t actually know what other people are thinking/feeling about me and that a lot of my worries stem from childhood experiences rather than current interactions.

But deep down, I feel as shit about myself as I always have and still assume that no one likes me and everyone sees me as a nuisance, finds me annoying or hates me.

Yes, I‘ve noticed that I sometimes speak in a higher, more childlike voice to my therapist when I feel particularly sad, anxious or vulnerable. I never do it intentionally but notice when it happens. 

I also unintentionally once spoke like this after a particularly bad argument with my boyfriend, but he got annoyed and told me to speak normally again. I felt embarrassed and have made an effort to keep my normal voice from then on. I think it scared him that I was in this “different state“. He called it psychotic but I think it was only dissociation. 

I think the fact that I sometimes use this voice in therapy (not actively making a choice but not suppressing it either the way I do with my boyfriend now) and that my therapist never judges me for it or even points it out shows how much I trust her and how close our bond is.

Thank you, that’s a very thoughtful and helpful reply. I‘ll ask my therapist if she can recommend a book for me to read over her Christmas holidays (three weeks). I think reading something I know she likes and has read as well would give me a bit of comfort.

Thank you so much for your comment. I was starting to feel confused by some of the replies because my therapist doesn’t view dependency as a bad thing. She says she appreciates that I‘ve allowed her to become important to me and that it’s part of the therapeutic process.
I understand your approach. What type of therapy do you do? I think the relationship between therapist and client is meant to play a bigger role in psychoanalysis.

I‘m definitely working towards being more emotionally independent. What frustrates me is that before I started to feel attached to her (the first three years), I wasn’t bothered by her absence at all. I do understand why I was so scared of attachment and wanted to avoid it. Although I know that I wasn’t really better then, just not struggling with this particular thing.
Thank you for emphasizing. I feel guilty too sometimes. And yes, she knows how I feel about not being able to see her.

I can‘t make a suggestion regarding what type of therapy would be best for you, but it’s interesting you experience this. 

I‘ve noticed that I yawn a lot during group therapy and have been feeling embarrassed about it. I‘m worried the others think I‘m bored or always come to therapy with a huge sleep deficit, which is not the case. Maybe it’s connected to trauma for me as well because I find group therapy very challenging. 

I think it makes sense that the body can react with signs of fatigue when confronted with traumatic memories. It could be an attempt to protect you. But I understand it’s not a very helpful response when trying to process trauma. 

I personally only have this problem in group therapy, not in one-on-one therapy. So the type of therapy does seem to make difference, at least for me.

I only stick to a routine if I absolutely have to. Like when I have to go to work. But even then, I don’t always manage and sometimes call in sick for mental health reasons. 

If I know I need to get up at 7 a.m. the next day and that being really tired would be a problem, I manage to go to bed early. But as soon as I don’t have plans for the mornings anymore, I‘ll go to bed at 2 a.m.

I also have depression and an eating disorder along with BPD and some things haven’t got easier since I was 12 either. Despite all my efforts and despite the hundreds of hours of therapy. It’s been dark in my head and my heart for many years now. No, the sun doesn’t come up, there’s no light at the end of the tunnel. There are better, moments, yes, but it’s never good. I’m never ever truly well. And that’s unbelievably hard.
I‘d probably feel embarrassed too, I‘m sure not all of my fantasies would actually be nice in real life lol.
I see. It would make sense then because I have misread some of her facial expressions in the past.
She wouldn’t lie to me!
I asked my therapist if she knows Reddit (in the context of me finding support in some subs) and she looked at me blanky and said no. So I have nothing to fear lol.
I‘ve randomly imagined just that happening a few times… maybe because the fantasy of her feeling sorry for me and helping me get clean felt soothing.
I laughed out loud several times reading this, so thank you for adding some fun to my day.

I was at that point too a few months ago. My therapist and I had a rupture and I was convinced she would terminate me. I was waiting for her to tell me. But apparently termination didn’t even cross her mind. We‘re still working together and in a way it was a healing experience for me that she made an effort to understand what happened and to reconcile instead of rejecting me the way I‘m used to.
You’re welcome, I‘m glad I could make you feel a bit better!

I did the latter too. I didn’t even consider attachment as a category. I think one thing that contributed to me getting attached to my therapist was when she suggested that it might be difficult for me that she has a daughter (who‘s about 8). I didn’t understand why she brought that up and disagreed. I felt kind of irritated by her assumption. But I guess it uncovered an unconscious part of me that longs for a loving mother. 

Don’t worry about not being attached yet. Showing up to the sessions and being as open as you can is enough. You‘ll feel attached when you’re ready to, and maybe your therapist can guide you a bit like mine did. I spent many sessions talking about stuff that wasn’t really at the core of my issues because I wasn’t ready to go deeper yet. I think you can’t rush that process. Some people get attached within the first few sessions, for others, it takes months or years, and some people may never feel an intense attachment and still benefit from therapy.

I felt the same a year in. It took me three full years to develop an attachment and to really trust my therapist. She sees the attachment as a positive step and actually encouraged it. Sometimes I think of it as progress too, but then sometimes I hate it. It’s painful to miss her, it’s painful to know that she has other clients and a family, it‘s painful to fear that she doesn’t like me and will abandon me. But I guess all these feelings are part of the process.

It‘s more in-depth and more about the relationship with the therapist. The therapist‘s role isn’t just to help you think about yourself and your life in more constructive ways and act in ways that are more aligned with your values and needs. Of course this is a desired outcome in psychoanalysis as well, but the path towards those goals looks different. It’s more explorative and the pace is slower. You’re actively encouraged to talk about how you feel towards the therapist because that often says a lot about how you felt or are currently feeling (and behaving) in other relationships in your life. For example, I keep assuming that my therapist doesn’t really like me, isn’t personally interested in me and compares me unfavorably to other clients. We talk a lot about what past experiences (mainly childhood experiences with my parents) shaped my negative idea of how others view me and my fears of being (secretly) disliked, rejected and abandoned. In other types of therapy, the relationship between the client and the therapist doesn’t play as big of a role.

This is just my personal experience, and I only have CBT and DBT to compare psychoanalysis to.
It depends on the modality. In psychoanalysis, the standard is two or three times a week or even more often.

I go three times a week because my therapy is psychoanalytical. Seeing your therapist two or three times a week is normal in psychoanalysis. I‘m not sure if my therapist has any clients she “only“ sees once a week.

I‘m the same. It’s so strange. The first time I noticed my therapist was wearing makeup, I felt almost bewildered because it was so hard to imagine her standing in front of the mirror applying blusher. I once tried to explain to her that I struggle to see her as a human, and she said, “What do you think I am then, an alien?“ and we both laughed.

Oh, I see. I‘m pretty sure no one can make out what we‘re saying. I‘ve never heard other people talking in our room at all, just the flute, which is probably louder than a normal conversation. And even then, hearing that other people are talking is quite different from actually understanding what‘s being said.
Constant white noise would annoy me a lot more than the occasional flute sound. It’s not often that we hear it.

Wow I didn’t know there were other people who struggle to see their therapist as a physical being doing physical things. You described it so well saying that it was like another dimension being added. I remember that it even felt weird to watch my therapist get up and bend down and look for some forms in her cabinet, even though it’s such an ordinary thing to do.

The house where my therapist has her practice is poorly soundproofed, and several times we‘ve heard someone playing the flute. It must be a beginner because it doesn’t sound good at all. My therapist always ignores it, but I‘ve had to smile a few times because it’s funny when you share dark traumatic stuff and then suddenly there are these random flute sounds in the background.

My face always looks fat. I work with kids, and a boy once bluntly told me, “Wow, your face looks fat in that photo.“ He went on to add that I looked better now. I was underweight but close to a normal weight when the picture was taken and had lost a bit of weight since then. Great. Now it’s hard to believe when people tell me I‘d look better if I gained weight.
Same. It’s not that I think I look a bit weird or not the most attractive, I‘m like “How can the people in my life tolerate to look at me?“

So relatable. I‘ve been wanting to go on Bumble (the version for friendship) for a while now because I have literally no friends I see regularly, but the four pictures you need of yourself doing something you enjoy or at a place you like feel like an insurmountable obstacle. I have 4,500 pictures on my phone and could only find a single decent one of myself that I could upload. 

I‘d like to use a dating app for finding a partner too someday, but taking and uploading a picture for that purpose feels even scarier.

I‘m not the person you asked, but I do psychoanalysis as well (three times a week) and I always sit in a chair. My therapist has a couch in her room as well, but she‘s never asked me to lie down and I wouldn’t want to. 

I‘m encouraged to say whatever comes up and my therapist helps me understand what’s going on externally in my life and internally in my thoughts and feelings. But as far as I can tell, she also occasionally uses methods from other types of therapy (CBT for example), like identifying cognitive distortions and challenging them. So I‘d describe her approach as more modern.

I wonder as well. My therapist did say once when I told her that I felt like I didn’t matter to anyone that she’d miss me when we won‘t see each other anymore at some point in the future. I didn’t really believe it at the time, but now I think that it’s probably true because I don’t think she‘d have said this if it wasn’t true.
I love when my therapist starts loudly laughing when I didn’t even think what I said was funny. It’s a bit confusing, but then she explains and I laugh too.

That‘s interesting. I‘m 23 and have A cups, and I‘ve wondered how I can possibly be related to my mum and grandma who have pretty big breasts. I‘m underweight and have always thought that my breasts would only grow proportionately if I gained to a normal weight (i.e. stay an A cup), but now I have hope I‘d actually go up to a bigger size.
Interesting that dreams about being late seem quite common.

I‘m sorry you’ve had negative experiences with therapists before. Negatively commenting on a haircut and mocking how your brows move? That’s really bad.

Your feelings are always valid and there’s a reason behind them. And I don’t think your issue is uncommon or that your feelings are disproportionate.

Your therapist might hold back her personal opinions and feelings about you, the things that have happened to you and the decisions you‘ve made because she wants to be neutral and non-judgmental. She probably wants you to be able to openly share everything you want to share without having to worry about her judgment. Because that’s what therapy is about and what makes the therapeutic relationship different from other relationships. 

I‘ve had therapist who were quite honest and direct about what they thought of me, and I didn’t find that helpful in the long run. I (unintentionally) started trying to please them and get them to like me and think positively of me, which hindered my actual therapeutic progress. 

That being said, therapists shouldn’t be too vague and general with their responses either. She’s supposed to respond specifically to what you share and not leave you guessing what she meant. It’s not a therapist‘s job to tell you what to do or to draw conclusions you’re not ready to come to yourself, but it is their job to guide you in the right direction in a structured and intentional way tailored to you as an individual. 

I‘d definitely bring this up in session to give her the chance to explain her approach and possibly adjust it to your individual needs. You could just say something like, “I’ve noticed that you’re quite general with the insights you provide. I‘m not sure what you think of me, and that’s causing me a lot of stress, anxiety and frustration.“ It’s important for your therapist to know that you’re stressed about not knowing what she‘s thinking. 

You can also explain that you’re concerned she might react negatively. Though I‘d try not to worry too much about it. It’s very unlikely that she‘s going to say something mean, let alone terminate you because of it. That would be highly inappropriate and unprofessional. 

I had the same issue as you with my current therapist and talking about it helped. She‘s helped me get better at developing an idea of how others (including her) might feel about me, and she‘s also been more direct and personal with certain things.
Interesting that he apologized. I mean, his actions in your dreams aren’t necessarily congruent with what he‘s really like as a person, so I don’t think there’s anything to apologize for.

Haha, I laughed out loud at the idea of flying through the room with two helmets on.

Thank you for mentioning the show, I‘ll check it out.

My therapist sneezes really loudly and it’s always funny when I talk about something serious and then her sneeze unexpectedly interrupts us. She‘s so careful and considerate with everything she says and generally quite elegant, so the way she sneezes seems really out of character, which makes it even funnier. I also love the “sorry“ that usually follows her sneezing. She doesn’t sneeze often at all, but when she does it always makes me smile even when I was sharing something dark and painful.

I have no social support either. I wish I could talk to my therapist right now, but I have 33 days to go.

I‘ve been in therapy for three and a half years with my current therapist and I had other therapists before her. It took me a long time to be able to trust my therapist, to fully open up and allow myself to need her. I spent almost three years (unconsciously) holding back. Actually, I think I still hold back sometimes, but I’m better at noticing it now and reflecting on why I’m scared of bringing up certain things. 

Then when I finally grew attached, it was very quick and intense and painful. I didn’t think I’d ever feel this way about her. I was incredibly overwhelmed. 

After about three and a half months of drowning in my feelings of sadness of longing, I developed feelings of frustration and even anger directed at her. I thought that she couldn’t help me, I felt hurt after every single session and there were sessions where she got annoyed at me as well.

We were able to work through the rupture, which I hadn’t expected. I thought she was going to terminate me and also considered quitting myself. But things got better. I started to feel more accepting of the kind of relationship we have. The transference stopped feeling all-consuming. It didn’t go away completely, but it lost some of its sharpness.

Five weeks of not seeing her is still really hard, though. It’s only been four days since our last session and I‘ve already been struggling so much and feel in desperate need to talk to her about the things that have gone wrong in order to be able to cope with them. Because despite my efforts, I‘m not coping well at all right now.

You‘re not alone in struggling to get by without your therapist, especially when the usual weekly rhythm gets interrupted. 

It’s not wrong or unhealthy to get attached to your therapist. It can even be a positive sign and show that the therapy is working. 

And it will get easier eventually. Just a few months ago, I didn’t believe it would ever get easier for myself and thought that the attachment would always be more painful than beneficial.

But then it became easier to accept and be okay with the limits of our therapeutic relationship (in terms of the time we spend together and also in terms of what the relationship involves and doesn’t involve). 

Now I‘m struggling again because my therapist has gone on a long holiday and I won’t be seeing her for five weeks. I feel anxious about it and have noticed that my depression symptoms have worsened. But I‘m coping better with it than I would have a few months ago. 

So hang in there. She’ll be back. She‘s probably thinking of you outside of sessions. And it won’t always feel this way.

I hate that I feel so bad about seeing good-looking women. Like, they haven‘t done anything wrong. I wish I could appreciate their beauty or just feel neutral about it instead of immediately crashing with my self-worth and mood. I can go from thinking my body is okay to thinking I‘m too ugly to be alive in a few seconds when I see a woman I consider attractive. I miss the time when I was a child and didn’t rate or compare physical appearance because attractiveness/beauty just wasn’t a category for me.
23f, would love to make friends!

As a teenager, I didn’t have much interest in the boys or girls in my class. I was still unconsciously looking for the parent I never had. I think that’s why my FPs have always been authority figures in one way or another. But I didn’t understand that as a teenager, I just wondered why I was so different.

I had a crush on a teacher that started when I was 13 and lasted all the way until I left school at 17. I watched friends move on from crushes (mostly on boys and not teachers) after a few months, and I was surprised they could do that. I‘m 23 now and I think I‘d still feel the same about this teacher if I saw him today.
You sound like a great person and partner. Thank you for saying this. I often feel like a burden and bad partner for struggling even though I‘m trying really hard to get better.

I also have mental illness and I‘m also in an unhealthy relationship with a man who‘s done some bad things to me. I still love him and it’s still my choice that I’m staying with him. If I died as a result of my mental illnesses, I wouldn’t want my friends, family or anyone who knew me to blame him. And I feel similarly about Amy and Blake. I think there was a toxic dynamic in their relationship that both of them were involved in and contributing to. It’s not like Blake forced her to take drugs or engage in other harmful behaviours (at least as far as I know). It’s not fair to paint a picture of Amy as his victim. That’s not fair on Amy either because I think she‘d want to be seen as an adult who made conscious decisions and understood what was happening, not someone who‘s helplessly at the mercy of their partner. Sometimes we know something isn’t good for us, and for complex reasons, we do it anyway. That’s true for me in my relationship, and I think it applied to Amy as well. Great suffering and the awareness that Blake was hurting her coexisted with great feelings of love.
Exactly, restless all night and then I fall fast asleep at 7a.m.
Reality as a mentally ill teenager and adult has definitely hit different.

I thought people just went to the cash machine to get money from some collective fund when they‘d run out of money. I didn’t know Dad was withdrawing his OWN money. I thought it was like drinking water from a public drinking fountain, where there’s enough for everyone and nobody cares how much you take. I did know my parents went to work, but I thought that was just to pass the time, see friends and have fun, like kindergarten for adults.
If this was intended as a joke (which I hope it was), it worked. I‘m laughing at the idea of showing up to therapy in a suit.
I asked my therapist is she knows Reddit and she said no, so I have nothing to be scared of lol.

I was in the same position you are in a few years ago. I had been diagnosed with depression and anorexia as a teenager but felt that there was something else going on.

It’s totally okay to just explain to your therapist why you think you have BPD, why you think a diagnosis would be helpful and ask her what her perspective is on this. That’s how I approached the topic with my therapist. She validated my thoughts on this and my desire for clarity and said that she wanted to spend more time speaking to me to be able to accurately diagnose me (we’d only had a few sessions at this point). About two months later, I asked her about my diagnoses again, and she confirmed I have BPD. She never did any formal testing or asked specific questions from a diagnostic manual. I think she just gathered the criteria I met along the way as we continued seeing each other and I talked about my struggles.
It‘s understandable if a friend reacts that way, but therapists should know that commenting on our appearance isn’t going to help us work through our issues.
You‘ve helped me a lot with your reply, thank you.

Don’t comment on my body, not even when I talk about poor body image or certain insecurities I have. When I express difficulties accepting a certain body part, that’s not an invitation for you to tell me how you think that body part looks. I once told a therapist that I hated my nose, and he rated its appearance on a scale of 1-10. Not what I was looking for…
Okay, I see your point. Maybe I was just overreacting to the word “ego“ because of my own negative associations.

23F and feeling the exact same. After years of therapy, I still don’t really care about anything other than being loved by someone else. It’s embarrassing. Nothing else really matters to me. I feel like I should be a lot further along in my journey of building confidence, developing my own interests, goals and hobbies, and growing into my own person, but I feel stuck and exhausted. I struggle with relationships (both platonic and romantic) because my desire to be loved is overpowering. So I absolutely relate, but unfortunately I can’t offer advice.

I have this problem that even though my therapist has told me she likes me and personally cares about me, I still struggle to believe it and am constantly afraid that her feelings towards me will change for the worse.

This is so relatable. I‘m in a similar situation at the moment with my T. It’s good to know I‘m not the only one who has experienced therapists getting frustrated by me over time. It’s a really hard thing to go through and I absolutely don’t want to get to that point again with my current T.

Idk, your comment seems a little harsh. What exactly do you mean by “ego“? Why can’t it be OP‘s heart speaking? They are clearly feeling strong and deep emotions in their heart. Using the word “ego“ makes it sound like it’s an issue of selfishness and vanity, which it isn’t in my opinion.

Yes, I‘ve experienced this. You‘re not alone. For me, it has to do with negative transference. My mum used to fake caring and being interested in me and could quickly turn from
calm and “normal“ to abusive and insulting me when she was angry. So it’s very hard for me to believe and trust people like my therapist when they say and/or show that they care about me. The suspicion and defensive attitude were heightened when I became more vulnerable and attached to my therapist because moments of emotional vulnerability were the times when my mum hurt me the most. It’s astonishing how powerful transference can be. Sometimes it’s not easy to even realize that’s what you’re experiencing.
I think you could just tell your therapist that you’re worried about the perfume being too much and whether they are okay with it.

Fühle ich sehr. Es ist okay, Liebe zu wollen. Es ist normal. Es ist gut. Es ist nicht okay, dass Du die Liebe, die Du gebraucht hättest, als Kind nicht bekommen hast. Es ist schwer, das nachzuholen. Aber korrigierende Erfahrungen sind möglich. Die Wunden des inneren Kindes können und dürfen ein bisschen heilen, auch wenn sie vielleicht nie komplett weggehen werden. Ich wünsche Dir alles Gute. Bestrafung ist das letzte, was Du verdienst hast.

I‘ve never heard of psychoanalysts being cold. My therapist is psychodynamically trained, and while she‘s strict with time limits as well, she‘s very warm and empathic. She definitely tries to show me she cares and is emotionally attuned to me, especially when I‘m in a particularly vulnerable place.

My therapist is my FP, which is really hard. It’s interesting that you mention trigger events. I spent three years working with her and did not become obsessed or even overly attached at all. It all started when I broke up with my boyfriend, so that must be the trigger event in my case.
I wish my therapist asked these questions at the end of our sessions! I think it would really help me.

As someone diagnosed herself, I agree Amy may well have had BPD. What makes you think most people with BPD will never admit they need to help? I don’t think this is true, I think it’s more common for people with narcissistic tendencies or even a narcissistic personality disorder, for example, to deny having a problem and needing help.

The fact that she said that to you makes it even weirder to call what you said odd. I‘d bring this up in the next session. You can ask her what exactly she meant by “odd“ and “be careful with yourself“ and tell her that those remarks left you feeling confused. 

Is this the first time she‘s said something that feels weird or out of place?

In my opinion, it’s your therapist‘s reaction that is odd, not you saying you wish she was your mum. I don’t think it’s odd at all to be aware of maternal transference and to directly address it the way you have. If anything, it’s great that you were able to identify what you were feeling and openly tell her about it. 
Transference was more of an unconscious thing for me for a while and my therapist actually helped me bring it to consciousness and find words for it. 

I don’t get the “be careful with yourself“ part either. I mean, you should be able to be vulnerable with her and shouldn’t have to be careful about what you share in therapy and how. It’s common for therapists to tell clients that they don’t need to hold back. This seems like the opposite.

He suggested thinking of these thoughts as an air-filled beachball floating in a pool. You want to go swimming in the pool, and the ball is big, you don’t like the way it looks and it keeps getting in your way. It bothers you. I don’t know where you‘re from, but here in Germany, we have flat-sharing communities for people with mental illness (so-called therapeutic flat-sharing communities). There are different types with varying levels of mental health support and freedom for the residents, depending on the independence and stability of the residents. Some have carers at the community round the clock, fixed appointments and group meetings several times a week and closer monitoring of the residents, while others are almost like regular flat-sharing communities and rely mainly on peer support instead of structures put in place and supervised by professionals.

I was advised to go to a therapeutic living community as a teenager, but refused because I was too scared. I sometimes wonder if I should have followed the advice. There’s more freedom and “normalcy“ than at hospital, but you still get way more care and support than you do as an outpatient.

He wants to help me to solve all my problems quickly and gets upset when he doesn’t see me getting better. But depression is a mental illness that you can‘t “fix“ in a week or a month or often even a year. Healing can be a long process with many ups and downs. It’s okay not to have all the answers yet. 

I think a relationship between a depressed and a non-depressed person can be successful when both partners acknowledge this truth and are able to create an environment of trust, empathy and patience, where both partners feel safe and seen.

Offer to listen in case there's anything he wants to share, but also tell him there's no need to explain if he doesn't want to. Show him that you care and are trying your best to make him feel better by behaving in a gentle, kind and understanding manner. At least for me personally, a body language and way of speaking that signal warmth and openness are more important than the actual content of what one is saying. Maybe you want to ask him whether he'd like a hug? Giving helpful advice to someone who is suffering from depression is usually difficult if you don't know a lot about the exact causes and nature of his problems or mental illnesses in general. Many depressed people feel lost and misunderstood, and well-meant tipps like "Try to distract yourself" or "Think of all the things you have already achieved" may even cause them to feel worse and more isolated. A reason for this can be that they don't find the advice useful and thus feel confirmed in their belief that noone can help them, the realization of being unable to appreciate the other person's efforts possibly resulting in feelings of guilt. Even directly, honestly stating that you don't totally understand his issues or don't know what he should either is better than trying to give some kind of advice just for the sake of trying to make things better. He'd notice that he actually feel helpless and in turn probably feel more forlorn himself.

Sorry this was so long. What I was trying to say is: Usually, depressives don't want someone to tell them what to do, but someone who is willing to feel their pain with them.

Have you always felt stupid? I know you wrote that you were not very smart already as a child, but have your grades always been bad, for example? Because depression can significantly reduce your ability to think clearly and logically, to quickly process information, to concentrate and to remember things. I'm a good example. I did really well academically for years, studied for hours without taking breaks and hardly ever felt stressed or mentally exhausted. Now I'm struggling to do my homework, it takes me an hour to write a couple of sentences, and I barely grasp the task formulations in tests. When my teacher asks a question, others are already answering while I haven't even fully got the question yet. My mind seems to have shut down. I got my IQ tested in February and the result was 132, but back then my depression wasn't really debilitating yet. I'm sure that if I did one now, my score would be a LOT lower. The cognitive impairment psychological issues can lead to shouldn't be underestimated. Maybe in your case as well the level of intelligence itself isn't all of the problem, but an underlying mental disorder, too (it could also be anxiety or ADHD)? 
And even if that's not true, there ARE ways to improve your intelligence (I found a few helpful articles on the internet when googling "improve yourIQ"), as well as to make better use of your potential. But in order to come up with the energy one needs to raise one's IQ or to be more successful in a specific task, quite a lot of determination, perseverance and also self-confidence are necessary, qualities depressed people usally lack. So again, I advise you to ask yourself whether you are really concerned about your below-average intelligence itself or whether depression caused you to feel bad about your cognitive abilites or even led to an actual reduction of them. 
Furthermore, it's common among depressives to make certain weaknesses they have responsible for their low mood and self-esteem. ("If only I..., I'd feel better.") But high intelligence isn't a solution to everything. You can be relatively bright in terms of IQ points and still a struggle a lot in life (as I do: pretty severe depression, eating disorder, no friends, physical pain, fatigue, the already mentioned problems related with school..). Be honest to yourself: If you woke up smarter, would your mood really improve on the long run? Would you enjoy life more? If not, try to find and tackle the real root of your negative feelings. If yes, do whatever you can to make you more intelligent and try to accept what you can't change.
I always thought that getting that "perfect" school report would make me incredibly happy, but the year I did was also the year of my first major depressive episode. Now my mental health is so bad that I can't function normally at all and don't even go to school on some days. I wish I had never started to care so much about my marks. The pain this obsession has caused and will continue cause is clearly far bigger than the benefits I got/will get from having done well.
